question: For a Class A or B CDL, when is a tank endorsement required for hauling a liquid or liquid gas?
choice_a: When tanks have an individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and an aggregate rated capacity of 1,000 gallons or more
choice_b: Only when the cargo is classified as a hazardous material
choice_c: Whenever any size container is permanently mounted to the chassis
choice_d: Only when the tank is constructed of steel rather than aluminum
explanation: A tank endorsement is required for a Class A or B CDL to haul a liquid or liquid gas in a tank or tanks with an individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and an aggregate rated capacity of 1,000 gallons or more attached to the vehicle or chassis; the liquid or gas does not have to be a hazardous material.
source_note: Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, introduction (tank endorsement requirement)

question: During a tank vehicle inspection, what should you check regarding manhole covers and vents?
choice_a: That the covers have gaskets and close correctly, and that the vents are kept clear so they work correctly
choice_b: That the covers are painted a reflective color
choice_c: That the vents are sealed shut with tape for transport
choice_d: That the manhole covers are removed before driving
explanation: When inspecting a tank vehicle, make sure manhole covers have gaskets and close correctly, and keep the vents clear so they work correctly.
source_note: Section 8.1 - Inspecting Tank Vehicles (manhole covers and vents)

question: Which items are examples of special purpose equipment you must check on a tank vehicle if it is equipped with them?
choice_a: Vapor recovery kits, grounding and bonding cables, emergency shut-off systems, and a built-in fire extinguisher
choice_b: Cruise control, power windows, and satellite radio
choice_c: Spare tires, jumper cables, and a tool box
explanation: If your tank vehicle has vapor recovery kits, grounding and bonding cables, emergency shut-off systems, or a built-in fire extinguisher, make sure each works; also never drive a tank vehicle with open valves or manhole covers.

question: When checking the intake, discharge, and cut-off valves on a tank vehicle, what must you confirm?
choice_a: That the valves are in the correct position before loading, unloading, or moving the vehicle
choice_b: That all valves are left fully open at all times
choice_c: That the valves are painted to match the tank
choice_d: That the valves have been removed for cleaning
explanation: As part of checking for leaks, make sure the intake, discharge, and cut-off valves are in the correct position before loading, unloading, or moving the vehicle.

question: What must a driver pay attention to when a liquid tank is divided into smaller tanks by bulkheads?
choice_a: Weight distribution when loading and unloading, so as not to put too much weight on the front or rear of the vehicle
choice_b: The color-coding of each bulkhead compartment
choice_c: Whether the bulkheads are removable for cargo flexibility
choice_d: Nothing extra; bulkheads have no effect on loading
explanation: Some liquid tanks are divided into several smaller tanks by bulkheads; when loading and unloading these smaller tanks, the driver must pay attention to weight distribution and avoid putting too much weight on the front or rear of the vehicle.

question: Even in a baffled tank, what type of surge can still occur and potentially cause a rollover?
choice_d: No surge of any kind can occur in a baffled tank
explanation: Baffles help control forward-and-backward liquid surge, but side-to-side surge can still occur in a baffled tank, and this can cause a rollover.

question: Because of the high center of gravity and liquid surge, how should a tank vehicle driver start, slow down, stop, turn, and change lanes?
choice_b: As quickly as possible to minimize surge duration
choice_c: It doesn't matter as long as speed limits are followed
choice_d: Only using engine braking, never the service brakes
explanation: Because of the high center of gravity and the surge of the liquid, a tank vehicle driver must start, slow down, and stop very smoothly, and also make smooth turns and lane changes.

question: What is the recommended technique for driving a tank vehicle through a curve?
choice_a: Slow down before entering the curve, then accelerate slightly through it, since the posted curve speed may be too fast for a tank vehicle
choice_b: Maintain constant speed through the entire curve
choice_c: Accelerate hard before the curve and brake in the middle of it
choice_d: Always match the posted speed limit exactly since it accounts for tank vehicles
explanation: Tank vehicle drivers should slow down before curves, then accelerate slightly through the curve; the posted speed for a curve may be too fast for a tank vehicle.

question: If a tank vehicle driver must make a quick stop to avoid a crash, what braking method should be used, and what added danger exists?
choice_a: Use controlled or stab braking; steering quickly while braking may cause the vehicle to roll over
choice_b: Slam on the brakes and turn the wheel sharply at the same time for the fastest stop
choice_c: Release the brakes completely and coast to a stop
choice_d: Downshift repeatedly without touching the brakes
explanation: If a tank vehicle driver must make a quick stop to avoid a crash, they should use controlled or stab braking; the manual also warns that if you steer quickly while braking, the vehicle may roll over.

question: On tank trailers, what can happen if the drive wheels or trailer wheels begin to skid from over-steering, over-accelerating, or over-braking?
choice_b: The tank will automatically vent to relieve pressure
choice_c: The trailer brakes will lock in the released position
choice_d: Nothing significant happens as long as the tank is baffled
explanation: Don't over-steer, over-accelerate, or over-brake, or your vehicle may skid; on tank trailers, if the drive wheels or trailer wheels begin to skid, the vehicle may jackknife, and you must act to restore traction.
